title: Papaya
wiki_lead:
The papaya (, US: ) is the plant species Carica papaya, one of the 3 accepted species in the genus Carica of the family Caricaceae.
It was first domesticated in Mesoamerica, within modern-day southern Mexico and Central America. It is grown in several countries in regions with a tropical climate. In 2024, India was the leading producer, accounting for 36% of the world total.
wiki_excerpt:
The papaya (, US: ) is the plant species Carica papaya, one of the 3 accepted species in the genus Carica of the family Caricaceae.
It was first domesticated in Mesoamerica, within modern-day southern Mexico and Central America. It is grown in several countries in regions with a tropical climate. In 2024, India was the leading producer, accounting for 36% of the world total.


Etymology and common names
The word papaya derives from the Arawakan languages of the West Indies, and is also the name for the plant. It was first used in English around 1600 in reference to the fruit and tree.
In some regions, such as Australia, it may be called papaw or pawpaw. In Australian English,  pawpaw and papaya denote the fruit of different cultivars of Carica papaya: the former for "larger fruits with yellow flesh" and the latter for "more elongated fruits with distinctively orange red flesh".
In the United States, papaw and pawpaw are names for a different plant and fruit, Asimina triloba, which is unrelated to the papaya.


Description
The papaya is a  large herbaceous plant, usually with a single stem growing from 5 to 10 m (16 to 33 ft) tall, with spirally arranged leaves confined to the top of the trunk. The lower trunk is conspicuously scarred where leaves and fruit were borne. The leaves are large, 50–70 cm (20–28 in) in diameter, deeply palmately lobed, with seven lobes. All plant parts contain latex in articulated laticifers.


Flowers
Papayas are dioecious. The flowers are five-parted and highly dimorphic; the male flowers have the stamens fused to the petals. There are two different types of papaya flowers. The female flowers have a superior ovary and five contorted petals loosely connected at the base.
Male and female flowers are borne in the leaf axils; the male flowers are in multiflowered dichasia, and the female ones are in few-flowered dichasia. The pollen grains are elongated and approximately 35 microns in length. The flowers are sweet-scented, open at night, and are wind- or insect-pollinated.


Fruit
The fruit is a large berry about 15–45 cm (6–17+3⁄4 in) long and 10–30 cm (4–11+3⁄4 in) in diameter. It is ripe when it feels soft (as soft as a ripe avocado or softer) and its skin has attained an amber to orange hue. Along the walls of the large central cavity are attached numerous black seeds.


Phytochemicals
Papaya skin, pulp, and seeds contain a variety of phytochemicals, including carotenoids and polyphenols, as well as benzyl isothiocyanates and benzyl glucosinates, with skin and pulp levels that increase during ripening. The carotenoids, lutein and beta-carotene, are prominent in the yellow skin, while lycopene is dominant in the red flesh (table). Papaya seeds also contain the cyanogenic substance prunasin. The green fruit contains papain, a cysteine protease enzyme used to tenderize meat (see below).


Distribution and habitat
Native to tropical regions in the Americas, papaya originates from southern Mexico and Central America. Papaya is also considered native to southern Florida, introduced by predecessors of the Calusa no later than AD 300. Spaniards introduced papaya to the Old World in the 16th century. Papaya cultivation is now nearly pantropical, spanning Hawaii, Central Africa, India, and Australia.
Wild populations of papaya are generally confined to naturally disturbed tropical forests. Papaya is found in abundance on Everglades hammocks following major hurricanes, but is otherwise infrequent. In the rain forests of southern Mexico, papaya thrives and reproduces quickly in canopy gaps while dying off in the mature closed-canopy forests.


Diseases


Viruses
Papaya ringspot virus is a well-known virus within plants in Florida. The first signs of the virus are yellowing and vein-clearing of younger leaves and mottling yellow leaves. Infected leaves may obtain blisters, roughen, or narrow, with blades sticking upwards from the middle of the leaves. The petioles and stems may develop dark green greasy streaks
grok_lead: The papaya ( Carica papaya) is a fast-growing, short-lived herbaceous perennial plant in the family Caricaceae, characterized by a single, unbranched trunk that reaches heights of 10 to 30 feet (3 to 9 meters), topped by a crown of large, deeply lobed, palmate leaves up to 3 feet (1 meter) in diameter. Native to the tropical lowlands of Mexico and Central America, it produces small, fragrant flowersâeither male, female, or hermaphroditicâand yields oblong to pear-shaped, melon-like fruits weighing 0.5 to 20 pounds (0.2 to 9 kilograms), with vibrant orange flesh surrounding a central cavity of black, peppery seeds; the skin ripens from green to yellow-orange. Widely cultivated in over 60 tropical and subtropical countries for its edible fruit, papaya thrives in well-drained soils with full sun and moderate rainfall (40â60 inches annually), often grown from seed and spaced 5â7 feet apart to support its rapid growth rate. Global production reached approximately 13.8 million metric tons in 2022, with India, Brazil, and Indonesia as the leading producers, accounting for a significant portion of the world's output and contributing to economic livelihoods in developing regions through fresh consumption, exports, and processing. The fruit is nutritionally rich, consisting of about 88% water, low in calories (43 per 100 grams), and high in vitamins A and Câproviding more vitamin C than orangesâalong with carbohydrates, fiber, and the proteolytic enzyme papain, which is extracted from its latex for use in meat tenderizers, digestive supplements, and pharmaceuticals. Ripe papaya is a low-acid fruit (pH 5.2â6.0) that may help alleviate symptoms of gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD), gas, bloating, and constipation due to its enzyme papain, which aids in protein digestion, reduces inflammation, and promotes gut health. Some clinical studies have shown significant improvements in bloating, constipation, and flatulence with papaya preparations, while there is some evidence suggesting reduced heartburn and GERD symptoms, although results for reflux are not always statistically significant. Papaya is consumed fresh, in juices, salads, and cooked dishes (especially unripe fruit in savory preparations), while its leaves and seeds have traditional medicinal applications for anti-inflammatory and antiparasitic effects, underscoring its role as both a staple food and a versatile crop in tropical agriculture.
